articles.title: Ontario premier wants Republicans to lose House and Senate over Trump's trade war
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he hopes Republicans lose the House and Senate in the midterms to hold President Donald Trump accountable for the trade war with Canada.
articles.body: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Thursday that he hopes Republicans in the U.S. lose both the House and Senate in the upcoming midterm elections, suggesting that voters should punish President Donald Trump for his moves to escalate the ongoing trade war with Canada. "Hopefully, he's going to lose the Senate. He's going to lose Congress. I hope so, and hold him accountable," Ford said. "But we'll see how that goes. We aren’t going to interfere in the U.S. election," he continued. Ford has become one of Trump’s most outspoken critics in Canada, accusing the president of attempting to move Ontario’s businesses and jobs across the border to the U.S. CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT "He’s not reliable at all," Ford said. "He could make a deal today and then change his mind. And we’ve seen that over and over again." Ford said he still believes Trump would like to reach a deal before the midterms and that Canada should return to the negotiation table as soon as possible. "I truly believe President Trump wants a deal before the midterms," Ford said. "I could be wrong, but I think it’s best that we sit down and get a deal." Ford’s comments come just days after the U.S. escalated the trade dispute by banning some Canadian dairy products and motorcycles as well most alcoholic beverages after Canada's retaliatory tariffs took effect on about $20 billion in U.S. goods. Trump also took efforts to remove Canadian products from large, long-term U.S. government contracts. Last year, Trump abruptly ended trade talks with Canada after the Ontario government broadcast an anti-tariff TV ad in the U.S., using quotes from former Republican President Ronald Reagan's criticism of tariffs. Trump and Ford have repeatedly exchanged personal jabs over the trade war. NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE Ford mocked Trump for keeping a portrait of Reagan near his desk while pushing for tariffs the former president had opposed, telling The Associated Press that Reagan would be "throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on." Trump, meanwhile, has criticized Ford as "the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford." The U.S. president further escalated tensions with Canada when he signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," a rebranding that Canada does not recognize. Canada, other international bodies and U.S. states are not forced to follow the renaming, but the order adds to the ongoing tensions between the two countries. Ford said on Thursday that Trump had unintentionally strengthened Canada by forcing it to cut its dependence on the U.S. "The only two good things Donald Trump has ever done for Canada" were that "he woke us up" and "he united the country like I’ve never seen before," Ford said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested on Thursday that his country may hold off on further retaliation against Trump’s latest trade measures, describing them as "relatively modest" compared to earlier U.S. moves. He said his government was still studying the U.S. measures and acknowledged they could have significant consequences for companies and industries, but he said that some of the new U.S. tariffs replaced others that the Trump administration had removed. "We also recognize that, in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done ... that these are relatively modest measures," Carney said at a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alberta. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats gain ground among Hispanic voters disenchanted with Trump
articles.summary: President Trump’s gains with Hispanic voters helped catapult him to the White House in 2024, raising questions about whether the key voting bloc had left the Democratic coalition. But less than two years later, Democrats appear to be making inroads with those voters, who are expressing dissatisfaction with Trump, the state of the economy and his immigration policies.…
articles.body:
President Trump’s gains with Hispanic voters helped catapult him to the White House in 2024, raising questions about whether the key voting bloc had left the Democratic coalition.

But less than two years later, Democrats appear to be making inroads with those voters, who are expressing dissatisfaction with Trump, the state of the economy and his immigration policies.

A string of recent polls show Hispanic voters who supported Trump in 2024 are being lured back to the Democratic Party, which could help it win both chambers of Congress in November.

A Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision poll out this week showed that Democrats hold a 23-point advantage among Latino voters in 17 competitive House districts, and 11 percent of self-proclaimed Trump voters said they will support a Democratic congressional candidate.

The move toward Democrats is playing into key races, too, according to the Cook Political Report.

In the Texas Senate race, for example, James Talarico (D) is beating Ken Paxton (R), 63 percent to 30 percent among likely Hispanic voters. In the Lone Star State’s gubernatorial race, Gina Hinojosa (D) is leading incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R), 60 percent to 33 percent. And Trump’s approval rating among Hispanic voters in the state is at 33 percent.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who spent Thursday campaigning in South Texas alongside Democratic congressional candidates, said the polls make sense based on the conversations he’s having on the ground.

“The top line is economics. People feel very, very, very stressed,” Gallego told The Hill in an interview on Thursday. “When I say stressed, I’m not saying they feel unhappy. I mean, they’re stressed.”

“They are literally worried about making bills, making payments. They’re complaining about the cost of everything going up: insurance, food, car parts, like everything you can talk about,” he said.

Luis Miranda, who served as the director of Hispanic media in the Obama White House, said the shift to Democrats is something that began last year.

“As early as last summer, Latinos were already expressing regret among those who had voted for Trump in 2024,” Miranda said. “This poll reinforces that those positions are hardening and affecting Trump allies on the ballot this year.”

Still, he cautioned that Latinos are “not a monolith, and Democrats will have to work to engage and mobilize these voters in ways that resonate with their communities in their states and districts,” including on the top issue, affordability.

“It’s an opportunity; it’s not a given,” he warned.

The new polling for Democrats comes as some in the party are warning they could jeopardize their gains with Hispanic voters amid growing influence of democratic socialists.

Some Democratic strategists say the “socialism” label could complicate the party’s efforts to win back Latino voters, especially in places like Florida, where the term has long carried political baggage with parts of the Hispanic communities there.

“Socialism is a nonstarter in places like Florida, where there are big swaths of Hispanic voters,” one Democratic strategist in the state said. “The word in and of itself is toxic.”

The strategist pointed to Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate, arguing that her membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) could hurt her with voters. Nixon joined the DSA earlier this year, but she has said she doesn’t agree with all of their positions.

Republicans, meanwhile, say the socialist label has given them an opening at a time when dissatisfaction with Trump on the economy has hurt them with Hispanic voters.

“They came to us because the economy was poor under [former President] Biden and people thought Trump was going to fix it and also that [former Vice President] Kamala Harris was not a great choice,” said one former Trump campaign aide. “It was a perfect storm.”

Now, the former aide said, winning back those Hispanic voters will mostly come down to the economy.

“If inflation were not so high right now, Hispanics would be in our camp,” the former aide said, adding that immigration is “not the poison pill” Democrats say it is.

But one thing is clear, the former aide added: “These are not voters who are locked into our coalition. And we may very well pay the price this election cycle.”

In the interview, Gallego — who was one of the few Democrats who performed well in the 2024 cycle partly because of his success with Hispanic voters — said Republicans “misread the Latino vote in 2024, as if they had just created a permanent coalition with Latino voters.”

“And they made the same mistake Democrats have done,” he said. “They just kind of took advantage of that voter. The Latino voter is fairly a swing voter. And they rented their vote to the Republican Party.”

In the lead-up to November, Gallego said, Democrats have to lean in on economic issues — particularly with Latino men.

“If we lean into …’This sucks. This economy sucks. We understand why you feel that way. We’re going to do everything we can to get out this,’ I think then you’ll be able to bring them back,” he said.

Looking ahead to 2028, Gallego said, Democrats will have to come up with economic plans in Congress that they’ll aim to pass in the next two years, “even if Donald Trump vetoes it.”

articles.title: A child’s memories of Sept. 11: Panic, debris ‘monsters’ and fleeing to safety
articles.summary: Twenty-five years have passed since the windows of my family’s apartment burst in and upended the life I knew in Battery Park City. My twin brother, Jacob, and I were just shy of 4 years old — we had already sent out invitations to our birthday party at Chelsea Piers — and were watching “Franklin”…
articles.body:
Twenty-five years have passed since the windows of my family’s apartment burst in and upended the life I knew in Battery Park City.

My twin brother, Jacob, and I were just shy of 4 years old — we had already sent out invitations to our birthday party at Chelsea Piers — and were watching “Franklin” on TV in the living room when we heard a loud boom.

On the other side of the apartment, my mom was jolted awake by what she said felt like an earthquake. She ran to her window, which faced the World Trade Center’s south tower — the second to be hit but the first to fall — and saw a “raging fire.”

“It was like ‘The Towering Inferno,’” my mom told me recently, when I asked her about her recollections of that day. “It’s not like you saw fire inside. You saw the flame coming out.”

Our housekeeper was panicking, holding my 2-year-old sister, Rachel, in her diaper. My mom called the fire department and was told to stay put. She called my dad, who was at work in midtown already, and he said to listen to the fire department. My mom hopped in the shower and came out to find her three kids on the treadmill in her bedroom, peering out the window to count the emergency vehicles filing in below. Both towers had been hit, but neither had yet fallen.

My memories from that day — some of the earliest I have — are spotty.

I remember counting 14 firetrucks below; I remember looking up in that moment to see an avalanche of debris heading toward us as the south tower began to fall; and I remember my mom telling us to follow her to the kitchen as the windows crashed in and darkness flooded the apartment.

But an almost-4-year-old’s memories are different from an adult’s — a truth I have come to understand as both a blessing and a curse.

I remember being chased by monsters — what I soon understood to be dust and debris from the collapsing tower — when we followed my mom to the kitchen. I remember my mom telling Jacob and me to stay there, as she frantically ran back to the bedroom to get Rachel — who, my mom later told me, she found clutching the bed, covered in glass. And I remember Jacob turning around to follow my mom, leaving me alone in the kitchen.

For years, my nightmares told a story of me standing alone in the kitchen, facing a monster as he crashed through our window. The individual moments happened — I stood alone in the kitchen and fled the dust clouds that burst in from the windows — but when I returned to the apartment years later, I was surprised to learn no window faced the kitchen. In fact, my mom told me she led us to the kitchen precisely because there were no windows.

Some time later — what could have been two minutes or 20 minutes — my housekeeper, Donna, found the front door amid the chaos.

She scooped me up while my mom carried Jacob and Rachel, and we all joined the stampede of people in the stairwell fleeing to safety as the darkness chased us down 21 flights of stairs. I was bigger than Jacob at the time and knew my mom could not feasibly carry all three children at once, but I remember the panic that set in when Donna took me from my mom in that moment.

We got to the lobby, and a retired police officer in our building had taken charge and directed us to the boiler room. My mom, still in her towel and biker shorts, tried to breastfeed Rachel, who wasn’t hungry. She was too stunned to eat, my mom said, and was barely moving.

Someone threw my mom a T-shirt to wear and a ripped sleeve for us to dunk in water and breathe through. I remember Jacob showing us how to use it properly.

When the north tower collapsed, the ceiling in the boiler room started to crack and we relocated to the mailroom. I remember telling my mom I needed to go to the bathroom. With limited options, I remember managing with a plastic bag that a dog walker gave us.

In many ways, a spotty memory of such a tragic event has been a gift.

I don’t remember the woman next to us in the boiler room, screaming, “We’re all going to die! We’re all going to die!” I don’t remember getting to the boardwalk — after it became clear we could no longer stay in the building — only to watch families ripped apart because there was no room on the evacuation van for everyone. Men were instructed to stay behind, and my mom remembers a single father parting with his daughter, pleading with the other women to keep his little girl safe.

I remember boarding a boat as we finally left Manhattan and headed for a shelter in New Jersey, but I don’t remember wondering, as my mom does, whether the boat would survive the short trip because so many people clawed their way onto the small vessel for their shot at safety.

I don’t remember the quiet sadness my mom talks about when she turned around on the boat to see her “whole neighborhood going up in flames.”

“You’re at what you think is safety — you are at safety — and you’re just overcome with the magnitude of the loss to see your whole neighborhood — we thought the whole neighborhood was destroyed,” she told me.

In the weeks after the attack, the buildings in the area were torn apart as law enforcement searched for evidence in the wreckage. My dad and grandfather returned with a suitcase and managed to salvage some of our belongings that hadn’t been destroyed. Being on the 21st floor, we managed to avoid the looting, but our neighbors closer to the ground were not so lucky.

For a while, it was difficult to track down our friends and find out what happened to them, if they survived.

But the following month, our birthday party proceeded as planned at Chelsea Piers — which had just reopened after it was set up as a temporary morgue — and our friends gathered for one final farewell.

Few of our close friends returned to live in Battery Park City after 9/11. We initially stayed with cousins in New Jersey, before moving to a hotel near my grandparents uptown. When Jacob asked my mom if “any more buildings are going to fall on us,” my parents decided to move to Westchester County.

But every year we returned, visiting the local shops that reopened and the shopkeepers who went back to work and never forgot us when we came back to say hello. And every year, we went back to remember.

articles.title: 9/11, Charlie Kirk anniversaries loom large for Gen Z
articles.summary: Raw reactions from older generations to the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, have stuck in the minds of millions of Generation Zers, most of whom weren’t or were barely alive when planes hit the twin towers and the Pentagon. The events of that day shaped the lives of those born after the terror attacks…
articles.body:
Raw reactions from older generations to the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, have stuck in the minds of millions of Generation Zers, most of whom weren’t or were barely alive when planes hit the twin towers and the Pentagon.

The events of that day shaped the lives of those born after the terror attacks and grew up watching U.S. troops fight in Iraq, Iran and Afghanistan. Gen Z and Generation Alpha have also lived through the threats from ISIS, al Qaeda and the Taliban.

It’s not surprising then that in a recent Gallup poll, 16 percent of Gen Z responded that 9/11 had permanently changed their way of life compared to 36 percent of millennials.

Thirty-three percent of Generation X, 29 percent of baby boomers and 15 percent of the Silent Generation said the same.

Gen Z walks a fine line between relating to 9/11 as a current event, as a historical event or holding a personal tie with the day.

Only 15 states require that students learn 9/11 in the curriculum, according to Joseph Kornhoff, executive director of the Pentagon Memorial Foundation (PMF).

“It was so fresh and raw that schools didn’t have time to put it into the curriculum, but here we are 25 years later and we’re looking at generations coming up and still not having that ability to learn about 9/11 from a historical perspective, from a personal stance,” Kornhoff told The Hill.

The National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial in Arlington, Va., is set to break ground on their education center on Saturday, with the goal of involving those from all generations.

Kornhoff, a millennial, says the terrorist attack inspired a generation of active-duty service members, including himself, who wanted to serve.

“I think it spurred a generation of our military. It was entirely volunteer force at that time and remains. You knew that you were going to be deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan within a year of enlisting or within a year of your commission as an officer … I think it was a catalyst towards a life of service for a lot of our nation,” he said.

Conversations with Gen Z, particularly Gen Z New Yorkers, reveal that reactions from family members to the horrific event are engrained in their minds.

“I don’t remember 9/11,” Bianca Pagano, 23, who was born and raised in Manhattan, told The Hill. “But I know exactly where my mom was and where my dad was.”

She described the day as “this visceral part of history,” which has permeated throughout American life.

“We’ve never known airports without security, like very immense security,” Pagano said.

“But also we’ve really never known a world where somebody’s ability to exist in the United States hasn’t been threatened one way or another by their own identity,” she continued, referring to racial profiling following the terrorist attacks.

This is one area Pagano feels Gen Z differs from older groups. She recalls hearing parents at her Irish Catholic school say that “thinking of people differently based on their ethnic background” was “perfectly okay.”

“I think amongst my generation, that’s changed a lot,” the Manhattan native said, pointing to the popularity of Zohran Mamdani (D), the first Muslim mayor of New York City.

When asked if Gen Z has a calamity it holds in its memory as strongly as older generations do 9/11, Pagano wasn’t sure. Maybe for Americans born between 1997 and 2012, there has yet to be such a singular catastrophe.

Pagano, however, offers another explanation: that perhaps younger generations have witnessed a buildup of other tragic events, like the mass shootings at Sandy Hook Elementary in Newtown, Conn., and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla.

“These events have lost their significance — not to downplay them because they’re extremely serious — but like we were so desensitized to them that it’s like, ‘F— no, I’m not going to remember where I was because it’s my everyday,’” she said.

Charlie Kirk’s large legacy divides Gen Z

When conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated at Utah Valley University (UVU) last year, online mockery was not tolerated — people even lost their jobs .

But in the weeks after his death, the internet culture shifted rapidly, driving the “memeification” of the late founder of Turning Point USA (TPUSA).

A song created by artificial intelligence called “We Are Charlie Kirk” began as a tribute but shifted in a meme that has been widely mocked. Others morphed Kirk’s face with the Mona Lisa and millions of other images, and people created websites that can “Kirkify ” any picture .

Kirk himself carried a massive social media presence, reaching his audience and opposition through livestreamed debates where he defended conservative social policies. The camera was rolling the moment he was shot on Sept. 10, 2025, and the video rapidly spread on the social platform X, which received millions of views.

How do tributes become memes, and how does something as serious as a murder caught on camera become something that is made light of? And what does all that mean a year after Kirk’s death?

Alex Turvy, a media sociologist and author of the upcoming internet culture book “Memes in the Machine,” said part of the dynamic comes from people on the internet feeling like they are being force-fed a certain narrative.

“When you try to force people to see something a certain way, they resist that,” Turvy told The Hill.

As some social media users resisted the veneration of Kirk’s legacy, they made jokes. AI and social media algorithms made it easy for this content to thrive.

“Whoever makes the weirdest, funniest, most unique joke gets rewarded with reach, which encourages more people to do that. It gets to a point where that’s most of what you see,” Turvy said.

Mario Nicoletto, who chairs the New York Young Republican Club’s campaigns committee, told The Hill he doesn’t understand the memes. “Let the man rest in peace,” he added.

To the 25-year-old Nicoletto, Kirk was a once-in-a-generation figure, and he remains shocked at the political violence that took his life.

Nicoletto, like other conservatives, places more blame on the left for political violence but also said he wanted the country to get over its political divides.

“I want to see Republicans win,” Nicoletto said. “But what I want more than that is to see Americans win.”

Young people in general are still divided over Kirk, just as they were when he was alive.

It’s no different at UVU. TPUSA hosted an event on its campus Thursday night in honor of Kirk, and the university canceled classes for the day and amped up security. But the conservative-leaning university has been split over the activist’s death. UVU’s Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) wrote an open letter that called for the event to be canceled. They also hosted a peaceful protest.

The university’s president, in response to criticism from the student group, said he would attend both the event and the protest to support all students, which led to more frustration.

Collin Grannis, a member of UVU’s SDS, told The Hill that by picking both sides, the university picked no sides.

“Charlie Kirk stood for being hateful and divisive. It’s not an issue you can have both sides on,” he said.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com , jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

articles.title: 9/11: The moment that changed the George W. Bush presidency
articles.summary: Twenty-five years ago today, I was in an elementary school in Florida with President George W. Bush, who was in the middle of a lesson with students when White House chief of staff Andy Card leaned over and whispered in his ear: “America is under attack.” That terrible truth transformed Bush from a sort of caretaker…
articles.body:
Twenty-five years ago today, I was in an elementary school in Florida with President George W. Bush, who was in the middle of a lesson with students when White House chief of staff Andy Card leaned over and whispered in his ear: “America is under attack.”

That terrible truth transformed Bush from a sort of caretaker president — whose biggest initiative had been limiting the use of embryonic stem cells — into a wartime commander in chief.

To that end, he branded Osama bin Laden, mastermind of the 9/11 attacks, “the evildoer.” Not to be outdone, bin Laden declared Bush “the head of international infidels.”

“The sword fell upon America,” bin Laden crowed from a rocky outcrop in Afghanistan as he celebrated the deaths of nearly 3,000 Americans. “Its greatest buildings were destroyed. America! Full of fear from its north to south, from its west to its east. Thank God for that.”

But America’s fear quickly morphed into sorrow and then anger. Bush’s first task was to reassure a reeling nation, although it took a few days for him to find his voice.

“We are here in the middle hour of our grief,” Bush told a hushed gathering at the National Cathedral in Washington three days after 9/11. “It is said that adversity introduces us to ourselves. This is true of a nation as well.”

That revealing introduction continued later that day as Bush traveled to Ground Zero in New York City, where he grabbed a bullhorn amid the rubble of the World Trade Center.

“I can hear you!” he hollered to the emergency workers. “And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!”

The crowd erupted in chants of “USA! USA!” Bush’s approval rating soon soared to 90 percent, the highest of any president, before or since.

Within two months, U.S.-led forces toppled the core of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Within four years, the first democratically elected Parliament in a generation convened in Kabul.

I was one of the reporters accompanying Vice President Dick Cheney as he witnessed the swearing-in of the Afghani lawmakers. It was an exotic collection of tribal leaders, warlords, refugees and ex-Mujahideen. There were women in dazzling colors and nomadic shepherds in heavy turbans.

Those were heady days for interventionists. By this point, democratization had become one of the central tenets of Bush’s foreign policy. The idea was that Middle Eastern dictatorships could be transformed into democracies — with a little help from Uncle Sam.

“There were certain people who said, ‘How dare you try to promote freedom,’ as if it’s like only available for certain kinda people,” Bush reflected this week. “It’s not America’s gift to the world. I happen to believe it’s the Almighty’s gift to every soul.”

The other tenet of Bush’s foreign policy was the doctrine of preemptive war. The argument was used to justify the ouster of another Middle Eastern dictator, Saddam Hussein, even though Iraq didn’t pose a particularly imminent threat at the time.

Critics in both parties, from President Trump to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), now deride U.S. intervention in Iraq and Afghanistan as “forever wars” of dubious value. But in the immediate aftermath of 9/11, Americans overwhelmingly supported military action against Afghanistan, which harbored bin Laden. Failure to retaliate was almost unthinkable.

But even after they were overthrown, Taliban forces never really gave up. Instead, they waged a 20-year insurgency against occupying U.S. troops, finally reclaiming power after America’s botched withdrawal five years ago.

By contrast, Iraq — despite plenty of ongoing challenges — is clearly a better place without Saddam. And yet Americans didn’t support this war as much as they did the one in Afghanistan.

So the legacy of 9/11 is complicated. As the father of a combat Marine who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan, I have mixed feelings about how things turned out.

Am I pleased that Saddam’s regime is no more? Absolutely. Am I dismayed that the Taliban is back in power? You bet.

But I’m also grateful that U.S. forces finally caught bin Laden after hunting him for a decade. And it still amazes me that for 25 years, we’ve managed to prevent another terrorist attack on the scale of 9/11.

Ironically, Trump came to power in no small part by deriding the “dumb wars” precipitated by 9/11. But in his second term, he has waged a preemptive military strike against Venezuela and launched a protracted war against Iran, urging its citizens to essentially help democratize yet another Middle Eastern dictatorship.

In other words, Bush’s twin doctrines of preemption and democratization may not be so obsolete after all. And while Trump has taken short-term political heat for his military adventures — especially in Iran — who’s to say such moves won’t eventually be viewed as justified?

“The job of historians is to put it all in perspective,” Bush told me nearly a quarter century ago. “We’ll let others make all the judgements [and] piece all the bits of the puzzle together.

“And in order to do it right,” he added, “there’s going to have to be enough time passed to understand.”

Sammon is SVP of editorial content at The Hill and NewsNation’s Washington bureau .

articles.title: Fetterman’s GOP convention appearance raises questions about his political future
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman’s (D-Pa.) surprise video appearance at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first-ever midterm convention is roiling Democrats in Washington, who are growing exasperated by his frequent Fox News appearances and criticisms of democratic socialists. Political strategists and analysts say that Fetterman’s low approval ratings among Democratic voters in Pennsylvania would have already made…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman’s (D-Pa.) surprise video appearance at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first-ever midterm convention is roiling Democrats in Washington, who are growing exasperated by his frequent Fox News appearances and criticisms of democratic socialists.

Political strategists and analysts say that Fetterman’s low approval ratings among Democratic voters in Pennsylvania would have already made it very difficult for him to win the state’s Democratic primary in 2028.

Now his video appearance at the Republicans’ convention in Texas is “pouring gasoline on the fire,” according to one Democratic strategist.

In fact, his audacious move to participate in the RNC’s convention signals he is unlikely to run again for the Senate as a Democrat.

“I’ve seen elected officials, especially ones here in Pennsylvania of all stripes, blasting Fetterman for this,” said Mike Mikus, a Democratic strategist based in Pittsburgh.

“With voters, I think he had already crossed the Rubicon into being completely unelectable in a Democratic primary. I think this just cements it even further. A year ago, I thought he was going to have big problems in a Democratic primary but would be able to survive if there were two or three opponents in a primary,” he said. “Now I see almost no way he ever wins a Democratic primary.”

Fetterman votes with the Democratic Party 90 percent of the time — something that he mentions when asked about whether he would leave the party — but he has also broken with Democrats on high-profile votes.

“Democratic primary voters I think are done with him and are going to walk away from him,” Mikus predicted.

A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll published last month showed only 23 percent of registered Democrats have a favorable opinion of the maverick senator — compared to 73 percent of registered Republicans.

The survey also showed Fetterman with strong support from independents. Nearly half, 49 percent, of Pennsylvania independents have a favorable opinion of Fetterman while 36 percent have an unfavorable view.

Mikus said Fetterman could run as an independent but warned it’s a tough thing to do in the Keystone State.

“It’s really tough in a state like Pennsylvania to win as an independent. You have so many signatures you have to get to get on a ballot. And quite frankly right now I think he’d pull more votes from a Republican than a Democrat, should he ever run,” he said.

However, Fetterman would also have a difficult time running as a Republican because, as he has noted, he aligns with the Democratic Party on most major issues by being “strongly pro-choice, pro-weed, pro-LGBT, pro-SNAP, pro-labor.”

Fetterman’s willingness to buck the partisan shirts-versus-skins divide in Washington has made him popular with Republicans at home, as well as with independent voters, who are a fast-growing bloc of the electorate in Pennsylvania.

But the decision to make a high-profile cameo appearance at the RNC’s convention — which was designed to boost Republican energy and turnout for the Nov. 3 midterm elections — is being viewed as a major provocation by some Democrats.

Berwood Yost, director of the Floyd Institute’s Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College, said Fetterman’s convention appearance puts him in a deeper hole with many Democratic voters.

“It is very hard for me to see how this — his appearance at this event — does anything to help him with that primary election constituency. The polling has been pretty clear, he’s lost support among Democrats, he’s definitely more popular among Republicans than Democrats,” he said. “That dynamic makes it very difficult to get elected in a primary election race.”

“It does the raise the question: What’s the strategy here? And the natural question is: Does he change parties? Is this a first step or another step in that process?” Yost continued.

“He says it’s not. He says he wouldn’t change parties whatever happens in the upcoming midterms and he’s a Democrat,” he said. “What he seems to be saying [is] that he’s tired of partisanship and most people are. … That is a bold risk to take, particularly if you do not intend to switch parties, and particularly if you do intend to run again.”

“The people who are angriest at this are his own co-partisans, particularly the more progressive wing of the party who thought they were getting a progressive warrior when he won his election” in 2022, Yost added.

Pennsylvania Rep. Madeleine Dean (D) called Fetterman’s convention cameo video a “stunt” and “gravely disappointing.”

“I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid,” Dean told reporters at a House Democratic event Thursday. “Those who went out and knocked doors for him — they are absolutely livid.”

Fellow Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan Boyle (D) grumbled over Fetterman’s appearance at the convention.

“A year ago I labeled John Fetterman ‘Trump’s favorite Democrat.’ Tonight, he yet again proves why,” he wrote on social media.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) told CNN’s Jake Tapper that “my constituents and folks all over Pennsylvania are pretty frustrated with John Fetterman.”

Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta (D) also took to social media to rip Fetterman’s video appearance.

Even so, Fetterman appears untroubled by the furor of fellow Democrats and even circulated a fundraising text on Thursday that springboarded off his controversial cameo.

The text included a link to an ActBlue fundraising webpage with Wednesday’s video of Fetterman embedded into it. It offered donors the chance to give between $5 and $250, or a custom amount, to help the senator “keep standing his ground, speaking his mind and putting Pennsylvania first.”

Fetterman described himself at the convention Wednesday as a “commonsense Democrat” who is “always going to stand with America” and “always going to reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life.”

His bold move to become a highlight at the Republican gathering in Dallas shows that he’s comfortable working with Trump and other Republicans.

This has fueled speculation that he may be angling for a post-Senate career as a straight-shooting political commentator on television or a future run for Senate or another office as an independent.

A Pennsylvania-based Democratic strategist who requested anonymity said that Keystone State Democrats do not expect Fetterman to run for reelection as a Democrat.

“There’s no sign that he’s going to run for reelection as a Democrat. The odds of him running for reelection as a Democrat are between slim and none — and slim just left the room,” the strategist said.

“There are slightly higher chances that he decides to run either as a Republican or as an independent, but I think the likeliest scenario is just … not running for reelection,” the source continued.

The strategist, however, warned that anyone “running as an independent statewide faces very long odds” because the state doesn’t have much of a tradition of electing third-party candidates.

Fetterman has not yet announced his reelection plans for 2028, the final year of his first term.

Fetterman said in a statement Wednesday that he’s a “lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly” with his party and reminded colleagues that he could wield a lot of power in a 50-50 Senate or a 51-seat Senate Democratic majority if Democrats pick up three or four seats in the midterm election.

“Should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” he said.

The potential that Fetterman could wield an outsized amount of influence in the next Congress is something not lost on other Senate Democrats, who were notably silent Thursday about Fetterman’s cameo at the Republicans’ convention — unlike House Democrats and local elected officials from the Keystone State.

“You’ve seen an outcry from a lot of the Democratic electeds but I think in a lot of ways it’s smart for the Democratic senators not to weigh in,” said Mikus.

articles.title: Trump officials blur Hatch Act lines with GOP convention speeches
articles.summary: Five years after top Trump officials were found in violation of the Hatch Act over their appearances at the 2020 Republican National Convention, President Trump’s Cabinet is once again taking the stage to boost Republicans ahead of the midterms. Administration officials have notably been introduced without their official titles for their speeches at the GOP…
articles.body:
Five years after top Trump officials were found in violation of the Hatch Act over their appearances at the 2020 Republican National Convention, President Trump’s Cabinet is once again taking the stage to boost Republicans ahead of the midterms.

Administration officials have notably been introduced without their official titles for their speeches at the GOP convention in Dallas.

Still, their appearances are a departure from the norms of government officials staying away from overtly political events — and highlight the toothlessness of a law that’s been flouted by both parties.

Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under former President George W. Bush, said he’s been pushing for a change to the Hatch Act for a long time, calling it a “charade.” The law prohibits federal executive branch employees, other than the president and vice president, from participating in some forms of political activity, like campaigning in an official capacity, fundraising or using their title to try and influence an election.

“It’s an invitation to trouble when half the time they wear their personal hat, half the time they wear their official hat,” he said.

A whole array of senior officials took the stage Wednesday night to kick off the RNC’s midterm convention in Dallas, including Attorney General Todd Blanche, Director of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Mehmet Oz, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.

Bessent and Rollins were introduced as “the honorable,” Blanche didn’t have any introduction and Oz was introduced as “trusted physician, author, educator and television personality.”

The second day featured a speech by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Scott Coffina, former associate counsel to the younger Bush, said using “the honorable” instead of an official’s title is advice he used to give.

“That’s how you address it when you’re trying to avoid a Hatch Act problem,” he said. “So, I think that they were certainly mindful of it.”

The officials talked about Trump’s accomplishments and warned of the damage the other party could do, but they stopped short of mentioning their agencies and the work they’ve done in an official capacity.

“If they start giving a speech that talks about the work of their agency and it’s extensive discussion of the work, of their agency, that’s a big problem,” Painter said. “Now if they want to get into foreign policy or whatever policy issues that are relevant to the work of their agency — all right, express their personal views.”

Blanche’s appearance at the convention drew the most attention. It was criticized by former Attorney General Eric Holder, who said before Blanche’s speech that the plan was “unprecedented” and “disgraceful.”

When asked for comment, the White House referred The Hill to comments made by the Justice Department’s rapid response social media page in response to a complaint from House Judiciary Democrats about the planned remarks.

“While Jack Smith may agree with you about violating federal law, the Hatch Act is available for everyone to read, and Todd Blanche’s appearance this evening in his personal capacity is legal (and has been approved by ethics),” the department’s official account on the social platform X posted Wednesday.

Blanche’s speech was short and focused on the administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration.

“It’s obviously unconventional for an attorney general to speak at a political event,” Coffina said. “They almost never do historically, but that doesn’t make it a violation if they do. And I just think he toed the line.”

Painter said Blanche speaking at the convention is not “itself a violation, but it’s symbolic that they’re willing to cast aside precedence.”

Violations of the Hatch Act are not new and are not exclusive to the Trump administration. Painter has said he has seen violations in the Obama, Biden and both Trump administrations, and he noted he was very critical of the Biden administration.

“Every administration goes through it, but the Trump administration has an attitude toward the rules, that the rules don’t apply to them, so it’s worse,” he said.

In 2021, the Office of Special Counsel determined that 13 senior Trump administration officials violated the Hatch Act during the 2020 campaign.

The report came out after those officials had left office, and there is no enforcement mechanism for the law in place after an official leaves office. Those in violation spanned from the former press secretary to the former chief of staff and former national security adviser.

Coffina said Hatch Act enforcement has “really become relaxed” over the years.

“The ultimate enforcer at the Cabinet level with a presidential appointee is the president,” he said. “So, if he decides to let it go, or sets a tone that it doesn’t matter, or that he’s going to have a high threshold for it … and that’s the pattern of the last three administrations.”

Painter has written op-eds and has testified before Congress calling for reform of the Hatch Act to make it so political appointees can’t engage in partisan politics while in office.

Change won’t come, he said, because Congress won’t vote for Hatch Act reform if their party is in the White House.

“Voters have got to get fed up and they have to say they want ethics in Washington,” he said.

articles.title: 25 years later, 9/11 memories endure as nation gathers to honor nearly 3,000 lives lost
articles.summary: Trump is expected to speak at the Pentagon ceremony as Ground Zero and the Flight 93 Memorial mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
articles.body: Ceremonies at the 9/11 Memorial in New York, the Pentagon and the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania will take place Friday as the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, when 19 al Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners and attacked the United States. Officials and others with memories of that day reflected on what they witnessed and what they lost in some cases as the nation mourns anew. Retired Maj. Gen. Bert Mizusawa, who served in senior Army positions at the Pentagon before 9/11, worked as a senior Pentagon official in the time leading up to 9/11 and knew several colleagues who perished that day. On that Tuesday, Mizusawa said he was watching coverage of the attack on the Twin Towers from his office when reporters broke in to say the Pentagon had been targeted. FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP’S 9/11 TRIBUTE TO FEATURE MASSIVE PIECE OF GROUND ZERO HISTORY AT WHITE HOUSE "I looked out my window and was able to observe the plume of smoke rising from the attack on the Pentagon," Mizusawa said. "My normal commute took me directly past the section that was destroyed, and the smoke lingered for days." Mizusawa, the GOP nominee for Senate against Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said he also played a role in hiring Army Lt. Gen. Timothy Maude, the highest-ranking military officer killed in the Pentagon attack. He added he just recently met with the lone survivor of the Pentagon's staff section that took a direct hit from American Airlines Flight 77 that day. "I reflected that, as tragic as the attack on the Pentagon was, the low-rise multi-ringed structure saved many lives as it was the virtual opposite form of structure compared to the World Trade Center buildings," he said. Warner similarly recalled watching the attacks unfold and seeing smoke rise from the Pentagon that day. "I vividly remember the September 11 attacks, and I watched the smoke rise above the Pentagon...," he said. "On the 25th anniversary of these tragic attacks, we remember the lives lost at the Pentagon, in Pennsylvania, and in New York City, and our brave first responders whose heroic actions saved countless lives." Also in Virginia, President Donald Trump is expected to attend the Pentagon’s ceremony. Trump has attended 9/11 observances at each of the three attack sites in different years. GOP SENATORS RALLY BEHIND 9/11 FAMILIES IN PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM ANNIVERSARY CEREMONY: 'HE'S A DISGRACE' In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani are expected to attend the solemn ceremony and reading-of-names at the World Trade Center site. Hochul’s opponent, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, told Fox News Digital that that day changed his home state and his family forever. "The pain has never completely gone away," Blakeman said. "My nephew Tommy was murdered while he was giving first aid to a severely burned woman. I lost many colleagues and friends on that day. We must never forget the danger facing our country from those with anti-American values." Tommy, a New York State Courts officer, was reportedly rendering aid to a victim when Tower Two collapsed on him. 9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD "The terrorist attacks on September 11 forever reshaped our city and state, and every year on the anniversary New Yorkers feel the weight of unimaginable tragedy and honor the lives lost," Hochul said, reflecting on the day. "In the aftermath of 9/11, New Yorkers showed the world what courage, sacrifice and bravery looked like," she added. Fox News Digital also reached out to Mamdani for comment. Former presidents George W. Bush, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden are expected to attend the 25th anniversary ceremony at the 9/11 Memorial in New York. Hillary Clinton, then a New York senator, is remembered from a photo with then-Gov. George Pataki and then-Mayor Rudolph Giuliani walking through the rubble after the attacks. Additional Trump administration officials will attend the third ceremony in Somerset County, Pennsylvania. Last year, Veterans Affairs Secretary Douglas Collins represented the administration there. The memorial is managed by the Department of the Interior, which said it will hold a reading of the names at 10:03 a.m. ET, the time United Flight 93 crashed into a field near U.S. Route 30 after passengers fought back against the hijackers. Fox News Digital reached out to Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Pennsylvania State Treasurer Stacy Garrity – Shapiro’s GOP opponent this fall -- for information on their plans for the day and comment on the 25th anniversary remembrance. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Garrity will be in attendance at the Flight 93 Memorial in her official capacity as Pennsylvania State Treasurer, her campaign said. Speaking as the GOP's gubernatorial nominee, Garrity told Fox News Digital she recalls September 11, 2001, as a bright September morning in the commonwealth that she and others thought would be a run-of-the-mill weekday. "But in the blink of an eye, in the skies over Lower Manhattan, along the shores of the Potomac, and in the fields of western Pennsylvania, our world was forever changed," Garrity said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Twenty-five years later, may God bless the heroes of Flight 93, the first responders to the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and every American who answered the call to serve that day and in the years to follow: Let’s roll," Garrity added, quoting Flight 93 victim Todd Beamer of Cranbury, N.J., who was recorded calling out that phrase as he led an unsuccessful effort to retake control of the plane from the terrorists.

articles.title: Shouts of ‘he should be shot’ heard during GOP midterm convention speech criticizing Democratic candidates
articles.summary: Shouts of “he should be shot” could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing promin...
articles.body:
Shouts of "he should be shot" could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing prominent Democratic politicians by name.

Cruz mentioned three Democrats — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. After each name, there were shouts audible on the broadcast of "He should be shot!"

It was unclear if Cruz heard the shouts, and representatives for the senator and the Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A spokesperson for Mike Rogers, the Republican running against El-Sayed, said in a statement that Rogers "condemns those comments — and all political violence."

But the shouts came on the same day that many Republicans denounced political violence on the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Vice President JD Vance, who was friends with Kirk, reflected on his killing in a headlining speech.

El-Sayed responded during an interview on CNN's "The Source with Kaitlan Collins."

"I'm a dad with two daughters and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad," he told Collins. "This is what has become norm in our politics. I mean, literally calls to violence."

He added that "everybody who heard" the shouts should condemn them.

Kirk, the co-founder of Turning Point USA, was shot and killed on a Utah college campus a year ago. He was 31.

"Charlie was killed one year ago today," RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said as the second day of convention speeches kicked off. "He believed in America and freedom and young people's courage to stand up and fight for the country they love."

Many of Thursday's speeches were otherwise devoted to attacking Democrats as ideologically radical. The shouts of "He should be shot!" could be heard while Cruz was telling Republicans to take seriously the past comments and positions of Mamdani, El-Sayed and Talarico.

"A simple truth: When people tell you who they are, believe them," Cruz said. "When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it."

"When Abdul El-Sayed says he has a, quote, 'obligation,' to comply with Sharia law, he means it," the Texas senator said.

"And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means it," Cruz said.

Mamdani, a democratic socialist, spoke about "the end goal of seizing the means of production" during a 2021 speech discussing his political beliefs, according to Politifact. When the comment came up during his 2025 mayoral campaign, a spokesperson said his platform did not include seizing the means of production.

Cruz's criticism of El-Sayed stems from a 2009 interview with The New York Times where El-Sayed, then a medical student, said he felt an "obligation" to follow Sharia law in buying his first home. Muslims are discouraged from paying interest on loans, which can make seeking out a mortgage more complicated.

And Cruz was calling out Talarico over a recent CNN report that he said in 2020 that capitalism needed to be "dismantl(ed)" along with White supremacy and climate change. Talarico's campaign said the Democrat was a "proud capitalist" in response to the CNN story.

Cruz brought up Kirk's killing during his speech while denouncing what he described as a rising tide of extremism in politics, one day before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

"The hate that killed Charlie Kirk, that knocked down the Twin Towers, that led to two assassination attempts on President Trump, it just gets keeping getting worse and worse," Cruz said.

El-Sayed agreed in the CNN interview that politics was becoming too consumed by hate.

"When you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us," he said. "I hope that everybody who heard that is going to call it out for what it is: a call for violence that ought to be condemned across the board."

Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the second highest-ranking Democrat in the House, condemned the shouts in an X post , saying "every single Republican" should as well. And Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, also weighed in, calling them "clear hate."

This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, America and Britain still stand stronger together
articles.summary: Away from the headlines, British and American officials work together every single day to combat terrorist financing, dismantle scam-center fraud and tackle cybercrime.
articles.body:
Twenty five years ago, I was a young British diplomat preparing for my first posting to the U.S. Like millions across the United Kingdom and around the world, I will never forget the horror of watching the bright blue skies of America darkened by an act of terror that claimed thousands of innocent lives.

The response to 9/11 became the backbone of my career, with my professional life shaped by the responsibility to protect our people. That journey has taken me from work at the heart of U.K. government in the fight against al Qaeda and the Islamic State to leading British missions in Kenya, Pakistan and now the U.S..

For the U.K., the attacks represented more than an assault on our closest ally. It was an attack on the values at the core of our open, tolerant democratic societies.

Addressing the nation that evening, President George W. Bush spoke for all of us: “America was targeted for attack because we’re the brightest beacon for freedom and opportunity in the world. And no one will keep that light from shining.”

The following day, NATO invoked Article Five for the first time, affirming that an attack on one member was an attack on all. British forces were among the first to deploy alongside American troops in Afghanistan. In the years that followed, 457 British service personnel made the ultimate sacrifice and never came home from that mission.

When I arrived in Washington in 2002, I witnessed how profoundly the post-9/11 era transformed transatlantic security cooperation on a scale not previously seen. Our intelligence agencies deepened information sharing. Law enforcement teams forged new partnerships. Together, Britain and the U.S. strengthened border security, enhanced aviation protection and expanded sanctions regimes.

Institutions such as the Department of Homeland Security and the U.K. Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre became central pillars of a new security architecture, bringing together intelligence and operational coordination.

The U.K.-U.S. Data Access Agreement gave authorities on both sides of the Atlantic timely and lawful cross-border access to critical data needed to prevent the most serious crimes.

Yet, as I reflect on the past quarter century, I am struck by how much the threat landscape has changed. The handrails that guided previous generations have largely disappeared.

Today, we face a world of hybrid threats, geopolitical instability and rapid technological change. Hostile state and non-state actors, cyber attacks and disinformation campaigns increasingly blur the line between peace and conflict. In her first public speech as Chief of MI6, Blaise Metreweli warned that the “front line is everywhere.” She is right.

But one constant endures: when the U.K. and the U.S. confront these challenges together as a true team of teams, we are stronger and safer than either of us could ever be alone.

That security partnership delivers real-world results every day. In the last year alone, U.K.-led investigations into a global network which drugged victims to facilitate sexual assault helped bring multiple offenders to justice in the U.S. and safeguard numerous Americans.

Our teams prevented a planned mass-casualty terrorism attack in the U.K. The successful prosecution relied on evidence obtained through the U.K.-U.S. Data Access Agreement.

Working together, the U.K. convicted key members of the Scattered Spider cybercrime network, one of whom the U.S. has linked to more than 120 attacks and $115 million in ransom payments.

This summer, our teams worked side by side to help protect fans and players at the FIFA World Cup, with a focus on preventing drone attacks.

Away from the headlines, British and American officials work together every single day to combat terrorist financing, dismantle scam-center fraud and tackle cybercrime. We continue to conduct military operations to disrupt terrorist activity.

Looking ahead, we have an opportunity not merely to respond to threats, but to stay ahead of them as force multipliers.

Building on the U.K.-U.S. Technology Prosperity Deal, we have a golden opportunity to harness the combined strengths of our trillion-dollar technology sectors and out innovate those who would challenge our security and prosperity.

The Five Eyes partnership remains at the cutting edge of intelligence and technology sharing to help stop threats before they unfold.

NATO defends the North Atlantic, the US eastern seaboard, and the High North, while extending U.S. reach through the combined strength of its Allies. The UK is already NATO’s third-highest defence spender in cash terms and has committed an additional $20 billion in funding to a defence plan that’s set to spend $393 billion over the next four years.

Meanwhile, our trilateral AUKUS partnership with Australia represents another important step forward. As it approaches its fifth anniversary this month, it stands as a generational investment in deterrence and technological warfighting cooperation.

Among the nearly 3,000 people murdered on Sept. 11, 2001 were citizens from many backgrounds and faiths, including 67 Britons. Today, we remember them all: the victims, the first responders, the medical personnel and the servicemen and women who gave so much.

As America celebrates its 250th year, the lesson of 9/11 remains as relevant as ever. Freedom must be defended, security must be shared and the transatlantic alliance remains our greatest source of strength.

Sir Christian Turner is the British ambassador to the U.S .

articles.title: I bought an opioid at the gas station, and it was legal. That’s a problem.
articles.summary: A surgeon cannot give a patient three days of pain relief without creating a paper trail, but anyone can buy a substance 13 times as strong as morphine along with their breakfast taquito.
articles.body:
I walked into a gas station last week and bought an opioid. Not something “kind of like an opioid.” Not a supplement that makes you sleepy. An opioid, in the pharmacological sense, that hits the same receptor in your brain as oxycodone and fentanyl.

To be clear this product would not test like an opioid — which is a huge problem in and of itself. But our federal government explicitly refers to it as an “opioid,” and for good reason.

I made the purchase on purpose, because I wanted to see if I could. It took all of ninety seconds. The clerk rang it up between a coca cola and some beef jerky for my dog. He never even looked up.

I threw it in the trash in the parking lot — I am a statistician, not a drug-user. But I wanted to know what someone with twenty dollars and a curious afternoon could get his hands on. Now I know.

I must acknowledge that some people say that it is not an opioid, even though the FDA and the Secretary of HHS contradict this position. The FDA’s own scientific assessment classifies it as an opioid. You can decide for yourself.

7-OH — short for 7-hydroxymitragynine — is one of the dozens of alkaloids in kratom, a Southeast Asian tree whose leaves people have chewed for centuries. Japanese chemists identified it in the early 1990s. For about thirty years, nobody outside a pharmacology lab cared about it.

In the leaf, it exists in trace amounts — a fraction of a percent. But the stuff on gas station shelves is not the leaf. It is made by taking kratom extract and chemically oxidizing it. A compound the plant barely produces is now the main ingredient. Then it gets pressed into tablets and gummies and little drink shots, with packaging that looks like an energy drink had a baby with a candy bar.

In studies, 7-OH binds to the mu-opioid receptor with a potency reported at up to 13 times that of morphine . The FDA commissioner said that figure out loud in July 2025. That is not “sort of” an opioid. That is a very serious opioid, and it is being sold in cherry flavor next to the chewing gum.

First, whoever figured out that you could take a 30-year-old footnote in the chemistry literature, concentrate it, put it in a gummy, and sell it legally in 40-some states deserves some kind of dark genius award. Because that is exactly what happened.

Around 2023, the products started appearing. By 2024, they were in convenience stores across the country. Poison control calls spiked. Nobody had to smuggle anything across a border — they just put it on a shelf. And just as importantly, while it is an opioid in the pharmacological sense, it doesn’t test like one. If you take a drug test and are taking this substance, it won’t show up . Standard opioid drug panels don’t screen for it. For anyone who has to take a drug test for work, you can be as high as a kite and work will never know.

Second — and this is the part that actually makes me upset — look at what we did to everyone else. For a decade, this country has treated prescription opioids like radioactive waste. We built prescription monitoring databases. We capped pill counts. We made doctors so frightened of writing prescriptions that people fresh out of surgery — people with cancer — are told to take ibuprofen and stop complaining. I have written about this before, and the emails I got from readers were heartbreaking.

And the data are clear: Prescription opioids are not what is driving the overdose crisis today. Illicit fentanyl is. We built an entire enforcement machine to fight this.

Meanwhile, an unregulated opioid walked in the front door of nearly every gas station in America, and nobody was watching, because it wasn’t a pill from a pharmacy. It was a “botanical.” It had a leaf on the label.

Let me repeat that: A surgeon cannot give a patient three days of pain relief without creating a paper trail, but anyone can buy a substance 13 times as strong as morphine along with their breakfast taquito.

Why? Because we regulated opioids by where they come from instead of what they do. If it comes from a doctor, it is presumed to be nefarious. But if it comes from a smoke shop with a cartoon on it, then it is presumed to be for wellness.

At least the federal government has noticed — sort of. The FDA formally recommended on July 29, 2025 that it be made a Schedule I drug. But the actual rule — the one that would take the tablets off the shelf, is still pending — more than a year later. In 14 months the FDA has gone from “this is a dangerous opioid” to “still thinking about it.”

Whereas surgeons have been all but forced to implement a no-opioid policy overnight. the DEA takes more than a year to remove candy-flavored opioids from gas stations in a year.

A handful of states got tired of waiting. Florida issued an emergency rule in 2025. Tennessee’s ban kicked in this July. Massachusetts, Kansas and North Dakota have also acted. But most states have not. Idaho, one of the only states that still bans marijuana for virtually all purposes, has no rules about it 7-OH at all.

The DEA should issue the scheduling order today — not tomorrow. It has had the FDA’s science for more than a year. There is nothing left to learn. Every state that has not acted should follow Florida rather than wait on Congress, which has a bill just sitting in committee.

The tablets I bought are in a trash can at a gas station, but the rest of the box is still on the shelf, right where I found it, under the fluorescent lights, between the energy shots and the phone chargers. Somebody is going to buy it tonight — probably somebody young.

I went in just to find out how easy it was. Here is the answer: It is easier to buy a 13-times-morphine opioid in this country than it is to buy a box of Sudafed. Figure that one out.

Liberty Vittert Capito is a professor of data science at Washington University in St. Louis and the resident on-air statistician for NewsNation.
